n: Chapters 29–32 contain seven oracles against Egypt. This first is dated January 587 BC, during Jerusalem’s siege, when Judah hoped Egypt would rescue it.

f.w: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, in the twelfth day

n: Ezekiel turns against Pharaoh (Hophra) and all Egypt.

f.g: Pharaoh Hophra (Apries), who briefly marched to help Jerusalem.

n: Pharaoh is pictured as a great crocodile (“dragon”) lying in the Nile channels, boasting, “The Nile is mine; I made it for myself.” He claims credit that belongs to God.

f.g: Hebrew tannin—a sea monster or crocodile.

n: God will hook him by the jaws like a captured crocodile and drag him out, with the fish of the Nile (Egypt’s people) clinging to his scales.

f.w: I will put hooks in thy jaws

n: He will be tossed into the desert to rot, unburied, food for animals and birds—a shameful end in a culture that prized burial.

f.w: thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered

n: Egypt has been a “staff of reed” for Israel—something that looks supportive but snaps when leaned on.
When Israel grabbed hold of Egypt, it splintered, tearing their shoulders and making their backs give way. Trusting in the world instead of God leaves us wounded.

f.w: when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest

n: God will bring a sword against Egypt and cut off people and animals.

f.w: I will bring a sword upon thee

n: Egypt will be ruined because of Pharaoh’s boast that he made the Nile.

f.w: The river is mine, and I have made it

n: God will lay Egypt waste from Migdol to Syene (Aswan) and to the border of Cush—its full length, north to south.

f.g: Better “from Migdol to Syene”—from Egypt’s northern frontier to Aswan in the south.
Hebrew Cush—the region of Nubia (modern Sudan).

n: Neither people nor animals will pass through for forty years—a symbolic generation of judgment, like Israel’s wilderness years.
Egypt will be desolate among desolate lands, and her people scattered among the nations.

f.w: I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations

n: Yet God will regather Egypt after forty years. Even toward foreign nations, his judgments include mercy.
He will bring them back to Pathros, their ancestral homeland, but as a humble kingdom.
Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms, never again ruling over other nations. Historically, after the Persian conquest, Egypt was mostly ruled by foreign powers for centuries.
Israel will no longer rely on Egypt—a reliance that only reminded God of their lack of faith.

f.w: which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance
f.g: Their trust in Egypt was itself a sin.

n: This is the latest dated prophecy in Ezekiel: the 27th year, about April 571 BC—sixteen years after the previous verse.

f.g: About 571 BC, the latest date in the book.

n: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for about 13 years until his soldiers’ heads were rubbed bald and shoulders raw from carrying loads—yet he gained little plunder. Ezekiel honestly records that the outcome at Tyre differed from what one might expect.

f.w: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled
f.g: From carrying baskets of earth for siege works.
Tyre apparently surrendered on terms after a long siege, leaving little to loot.

n: So God will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his army. Babylon did invade Egypt around 568 BC.

f.w: it shall be the wages for his army

n: Nebuchadnezzar unknowingly worked for God, so God pays him with Egypt. God directs even pagan empires.
On that day God will make a “horn” sprout for Israel—new strength, often understood as pointing toward a coming deliverer—and Ezekiel will speak freely among them.

f.w: cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth
